extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners / Office personnel (patent examiners) and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and articulating obviousness rejections (KSR-era) including rationales like simple substitution, analogous art, lead compound selection, use of known techniques, and treatment of secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference that discourages, criticizes, or warns against the combined use of elements may 'teach away' and thus deter a person of ordinary skill from combining references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reference's teaching is contrary to the proposed combination (e.g., warns that increased rigidity increases likelihood of failure), the reference can be found to teach away. Teaching away may preclude a conclusion of obviousness even if all claim elements are present in separate references. Example: Puno warned that rigidity increases chance of failure, so combining it with a compression member teaching rigidity was deterred. Evaluate collective teachings of the prior art and consider secondary evidence (failure by others, copying) that may support nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable result (KSR standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'predictable result' inquiry covers both the expectation that prior art elements are physically combinable and that the combination would have worked for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing obviousness, demonstrate not only physical combinability but also that the combination would have been expected to function for its intended purpose. Lack of predictable operability (or teachings that render the combination inoperative) undercuts obviousness. The Federal Circuit emphasized that predictable results include reasonable expectation of success, not absolute predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution rationale — required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on substitution of one known element for another, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate specific findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate: (1) that the prior art contained a device differing from the claimed device only by substitution of components; (2) that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) that a person of ordinary skill could have made the substitution and the results would have been predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary in the case. If any of these findings cannot be made, this substitution rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples: In re Fout (substituting distillation for aqueous extraction), Agrizap (substituting resistive switch for mechanical switch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported where there was a reasonable expectation of success in making the substitution or modification; absolute predictability is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the level of ordinary skill and the enabling content of the references. Examples: In re O'Farrell — despite unpredictability in molecular biology generally, detailed enabling teachings provided a reasonable expectation of success. Conversely, lack of predictability in the art can defeat a prima facie case (see Procter & Gamble v. Teva).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art / pertinence across fields
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference from a different field may be analogous art if it is reasonably pertinent to the problem to be solved by the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining whether a reference is applicable, consider the problem addressed rather than superficially limiting by field labels. A reference is analogous if it addresses a similar problem or is within the same field of endeavor; it need not be narrowly focused on the exact type of device. Example: ICON — folding bed art was analogous to folding treadmill because both addressed retaining/stabilizing a folding mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer teaching away from mere silence
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference does not teach away merely because it lacks an explicit endorsement of the proposed combination; affirmatively teaching that a combination is undesirable is required to show teaching away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the reference explicitly or implicitly discourages the proposed modification or combination. Arguments about inoperability must account for modifications a skilled artisan would make to adapt borrowed prior-art devices; inoperability assertions that ignore likely modifications are weak. See ICON discussion regarding inoperability and single-action vs dual-action springs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective evidence) and nexus
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence such as failure by others, copying, skepticism by experts, praise, commercial success, long-felt need, and unexpected results are secondary considerations that may support nonobviousness but require a nexus to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proffered objective evidence is commensurate with and tied to the full scope of the claims. Lack of coextensiveness between the evidence and the claimed invention reduces its weight. Examples: Muniauction (secondary considerations lacked nexus), Procter & Gamble (unexpected results and long-felt need weighed in favor of nonobviousness). Consider timing: long-felt need is assessed as of the filing date, not market date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead compound analysis in chemical obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: In chemical cases, obviousness based on structural similarity often involves identifying a 'lead compound' and a reason to select and modify it to arrive at the claimed compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should identify some motivation that would have led one of ordinary skill to select and modify a known compound (the 'lead compound') in a particular way. The requisite motivation can come from many sources and need not be explicit in the art. Structural similarity that creates a reasonable expectation of similar properties may suffice. Examples: Aventis (need not require explicit teaching to purify stereoisomer), Eisai (no reason to modify lead compound because modification would have destroyed advantageous property).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual meaning and limits of 'lead compound'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'lead compound' has varying contextual meanings; any known compound might serve as a lead compound for obviousness analysis, but there must be a reason to start with it other than mere existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that a compound inactive for pharmaceutical purposes might nonetheless serve as a lead compound if there is a reason unrelated to activity (e.g., structural, synthetic, or other technical reasons). There must be some articulated reason to select and modify the compound (see Altana, Eisai, Ortho-McNeil). Business considerations alone (cost, handling) do not constitute a proper reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical obviousness without a single lead compound
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness for a claimed chemical compound does not always require identification of a single lead compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness may be shown by prior art suggesting formation of compounds with specified moieties or by viewing the claimed compound as two known compounds linked together if there is a reason to make the linkage, a known means to do so, and a predictable result. Office personnel should consider such alternate theories where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of known technique to improve similar devices — required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on applying a known technique to improve similar devices, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate specific findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate: (1) the prior art contained a 'base' device that the claimed invention improves; (2) the prior art contained a 'comparable' device that had been improved in the same way; (3) one of ordinary skill could have applied the known improvement to the base device and the results would have been predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary. If any finding cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness. The rationale is that the enhancement method is part of ordinary capabilities of skilled artisans. If application of the technique would have been beyond skill, it is not obvious (KSR). Example: In re Nilssen (applying known overload protection techniques).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability and skill-of-the-art constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: If the actual application of a known technique would have been beyond the capabilities of a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time, the use-of-known-technique rationale cannot support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the technique was within ordinary skill and whether predictable results would have followed. KSR admonishes that mere assertion that a technique exists is insufficient if practical application would have been nonroutine or unpredictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results rebut obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected superior properties (e.g., potency, lower toxicity) compared to prior art can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document comparative tests and credible witness testimony showing unexpected properties. Unexpected results can be sufficient to rebut even a prima facie obviousness showing. Examples: Procter & Gamble v. Teva — risedronate had unexpectedly superior potency and safety profiles that rebutted obviousness.
